elements.name: mini-gateway
elements.description: A proxy that speaks the Postgres wire protocol (simple-query subset) in front of one Postgres: a hard-capped connection pool lent per transaction, per-tenant admission with two CoDel modes, read coalescing, an off-by-default retry policy, snapshot observability. Terminates client TLS; logs clients in with SCRAM-SHA-256. Runs as N independent instances.
plannedNotes: Built in chunk 6: a working proxy, the walking skeleton — cmd/mini-gateway terminates client TLS, logs clients in with SCRAM-SHA-256, lends a database connection per transaction, resets it after every lease, queues waiting requests, and serves health, stats and metrics from snapshots. Chunk 6a built the operator tools around it: the client mgctl, the load generator, the dev stack with its run targets, and the story report. Chunk 8 built the admission queues: one bounded queue per tenant with the two CoDel modes (the config file selects one), adaptive LIFO, and every shed request answered at once with 53M01. Chunk 7 built the pool: connections opened on demand under a hard cap and a creation limit, checked before reuse, cleaned up or closed when a lease ends badly, reset by one of two release policies, client cancels forwarded, one breaker that answers 53M03 while the database is down, TCP keepalive on the database sockets, and the connection and creation-rate budgets taken from the fleet block. Not built: fairness between tenants, the adaptive limit and the rate gate, read coalescing, the retry policy, the OTLP push, and the rest of the fleet configuration and the drain of N instances.

elements.name: End-to-end suite and load generator
elements.description: test/e2e; cmd/loadgen with internal/loadgen. Each scenario is written once and runs on the simulator (tier S) and on the real binary against a real Postgres (tier R), with the CSV flush on and SQL assertions over the files. elements.name: Transport seam
elements.description: The engine's contract with its driver, as plain events and actions (no Go interface). Events in: accepted, bytes arrived, bytes written, write refused, closed, dial failed, TLS result, cancel done, timer, publish. Actions out: write, close, start TLS, pause and resume reading, open a database connection, send a cancel request on a connection of its own, wake at a time, publish. Knows no protocol; its read rule (exactly 8 bytes of a new client, one unprocessed read per connection) keeps bytes from crossing a TLS upgrade. Two implementations: TCP in the shell, simulated streams in proxysim.

elements.name: Client session table
elements.description: One entry per client connection: its wire state machines, tenant, phase (startup, idle, queued, active, holding a connection), transaction status, the single request it may have inside the proxy, a bounded input buffer and the count of reply bytes not yet written. Caps the clients connected and the clients in startup. Keeps the map from proxy-issued key data to its client, which a cancel request is looked up in, and the idle-in-transaction deadline of a client that holds a connection (with the pool core).

elements.name: Database connection table
elements.description: One entry per database connection: its wire state machine, the query-cycle tracker, its phase (dialing, startup, idle, lent, resetting, checking, cleaning) and who holds it. With the pool core, every open and close is the core's decision and the phase mirrors the core's state. With the fixed set (tests only since chunk 7) the table keeps the set full itself: opens the configured number at start, one dial at a time, and dials again after a loss, after a short delay when the connect failed.

elements.name: Request pipeline
elements.description: The fixed order every request takes: classify, reject list, draining, breaker, rate gate, coalesce, queue, lease, forward, release. Each stage is counted as passed or refused, and each refusal is answered with its error-contract row: while the breaker is open, 53M03 at once and no dial. A queued request has a wait deadline, the outer bound whatever the queue rule; a request the queue sheds is answered at once with 53M01. A request waits only in the queue: a checkout that cannot lend leaves it there. Statements inside an open transaction skip from the reject list straight to forward on the connection the client already holds.

elements.name: Stage seams and stand-ins
elements.description: The small interfaces the pipeline calls: classifier, breaker, rate gate, coalescer, queue, pool, release policy, retry policy. The queue seam has an extension for a queue that sheds: remove, expire or refuse at an instant, sweep, next deadline, take the shed requests, put back a popped one, close. Also the stand-ins: a rate gate that always allows, no coalescing and retry off, used until their cores are built; and a breaker that is always closed, a fixed set of connections, reset after every lease and one bounded first-come queue, which an engine configured without the pool core or without a queue rule still uses (tests only: the config file always gives both). The engine's config can replace any of them.

elements.name: Lease end and reset
elements.description: A lease ends when a reply ends with status idle; while the status is in-transaction or failed the client keeps its connection. At release the policy answers reset, lend as is, or close (close when the status is not idle or bytes are left unread). The reset is DISCARD ALL sent as the proxy's own Query: the connection is lent again only after exactly that tag and status idle, with nothing after them, inside the reset deadline. Anything else closes it, counted by reason. Nothing of the reset's reply reaches a client. With the pool core the release is the core's: under on-switch a clean connection is tagged with its tenant and not reset until another tenant needs it; with lease.reseed on, a SELECT setseed follows DISCARD ALL and its reply is judged too; and a lease that does not end clean goes to the dirty-connection table instead of being closed.

elements.name: Reply relay
elements.description: Streams database messages to the client (or to every waiter of a shared read) as they arrive, through a bounded buffer per client, with back pressure in both directions: reading the database connection is paused while the client is behind, reading the client while its request is in progress. ErrorResponse and ReadyForQuery are held whole, so a FATAL from the database becomes an error-contract reply. Never sends a short reply that looks complete.
plannedNotes: Built in chunk 6 (internal/proxy: relay, relayEvents and relayed in lease.go; writeClient and the pauses in client.go): all of it for the one client of a reply. Not built: the fan-out to every waiter of a shared read (chunk 11).

elements.name: Failure classifier
elements.description: For every failure records whether the request may have reached the database (no only when the driver reports that its first write was refused with zero bytes accepted) and picks the error-contract row: 08006 for a safe read or when nothing reached, 08007 otherwise, FATAL 08006 when a transaction lost its connection (between statements, or mid-statement unless the message could have ended the transaction: then 08007), and a close with no message once part of the reply was sent. Hands the fact to the retry seam.

elements.name: Deadline table
elements.description: Every wait the engine has, as deadlines on the clock passed in with each event: one heap, and the next wake-up time returned as an action. The admission queues' next deadline is one timer in it, and the pool core's next deadline another. Timers due at or before an event's time fire before the event is processed, so whatever arrives at the instant of its deadline is late.

elements.name: Drain controller
elements.description: Sequences shutdown: stop admitting, finish transactions in progress within a bound, close idle connections, exit.
plannedNotes: Built in chunk 6 (internal/proxy: the EvDraining input, gates in lease.go, Shutdown in engine.go): while the draining input is on, new work from a client outside a transaction is refused with 53M05 and that client is closed after the reply (unit-tested; nothing in the binary sets it yet); and a plain stop that closes every client and connection. Not built: the sequence — finish transactions in progress within a bound, close idle connections, exit (chunk 13).

elements.name: Admission queue adapter
elements.description: internal/proxy/admission.go. Puts the admission queues behind the queue seam and its shedding extension. After every queue operation the engine takes the sheds the core decided, answers each at once with 53M01 and an end marker, and arms its one admission timer at the core's next deadline. With it no connection is lent directly: every request is pushed and popped, so the rule sees zero-wait requests too. At a stop it sweeps first and answers what was due, then removes the rest as client-gone. When the breaker opens it sweeps, then refuses every queued request in arrival order: each is a shed with reason breaker, answered 53M03. The engine's invariants require the core's shed count to equal the sheds answered.

elements.name: Pool core adapter
elements.description: internal/proxy/corepool.go. Puts the pool core behind the pool, breaker and release-policy seams and performs the actions the core returns: dial, the empty-query check, a cancel request, ROLLBACK, the reset with its re-seed, close, and refusing the queued requests with 53M03. It reports back every result, loss and lease end, drains a cancelled statement's reply, tells the core how many requests wait, and arms one timer at the core's next deadline. A client's cancel request goes to the connection that client holds; for a request still queued the client gets 57014 at once. A client idle inside a transaction past its deadline gets FATAL 25P03 and its connection is rolled back, reset and reused. The engine's invariants require every connection's phase to agree with the core after every event.

elements.name: Framer
elements.description: Ours. Cuts a byte stream into messages (type byte, 4-byte length, body) whatever the fragmentation, down to one byte at a time; also the untyped packets before startup. Enforces a maximum message size and refuses an oversized message from its header alone. Can skip the bodies of chosen message types instead of buffering them.

elements.name: Message coding
elements.description: Ours, written by hand, no pgproto3. Appends each message the session machines write (TLS and startup packets, authentication, parameter status, key data, ready, query, terminate, cancel) and parses the startup packet and its parameters.

elements.name: Codec boundary
elements.description: The only product code that may touch pgproto3: message structs encoded and decoded in one place. pgproto3's own blocking reader is not used. Nothing passes through it so far: the session machines, the trackers and the reply builders all use the hand-written message coding.

elements.name: Client session machine
elements.description: Client-facing, startup only: events in, actions out. Runs the exchange before startup: answers a TLS request S or N by client_tls.mode and asks its driver to start TLS (at most one upgrade; a byte before the handshake result is a violation), answers a GSS encryption request N. Reads the startup message, refuses plaintext when TLS is required, negotiates protocol 3.x down to 3.0, finds the tenant by user, runs SCRAM-SHA-256 (server side; trust only as a named test setting; an unknown user gets the wrong-password reply), sends the parameter set and proxy-issued key data, recognises cancel requests. Every failed startup ends under one reason. Consumes no byte after ready.

elements.name: Database session machine
elements.description: Database-facing, startup only: events in, actions out. Sends a TLS request first when backend_tls.mode asks for one (an N answer is a connect failure; a byte after S before the handshake result is a violation), then startup, SCRAM-SHA-256 (client side, never -PLUS), collects server parameters and key data, reaches ready. Every failed startup ends in one class (TLS refused or failed, authentication, too many connections, server FATAL, violation, deadline, connection lost).

elements.name: Query-cycle tracker
elements.description: Follows a reply to its ReadyForQuery, reports the transaction status byte (idle, in transaction, failed), flags an unsolicited ParameterStatus (the connection is now dirty) and any protocol surprise, including a stream that ends without its marker. Never buffers row data. Unknown but well-framed message types are reported and passed through.

elements.name: Client query-phase tracker
elements.description: Reads the client's bytes after login. Reports each Query (body copied, bounded), Terminate, and every extended-protocol message as one to refuse; any other message type is a violation.

elements.name: SCRAM-SHA-256 functions
elements.description: Pure functions on the standard library: verifier, key derivation, nonce, the GS2 header rule, and the server and client sides of the exchange with bounded messages. Shared with the simulator's fake Postgres and simulated clients.

elements.name: Startup FATAL replies
elements.description: The replies the session machines make themselves during startup: an ErrorResponse with severity, SQLSTATE and message, the old-format error for a protocol 2 client, and NegotiateProtocolVersion. Also parses the severity and SQLSTATE of an ErrorResponse from the database. The client session machine names a row of the error table for every FATAL it writes and takes the code from that row; the encoders stay here.

elements.name: Wire snapshot
elements.description: The wire layer's counters as one plain struct, per side: startups begun, completed, in progress and failed by reason; pre-startup requests by kind and answer; TLS handshakes by version and failure; plaintext refused; authentication failures by cause; messages and bytes each way; violations; oversized messages; what the trackers saw. Its check: begun = completed + failed + in startup, on each side.

elements.name: SQL lexer
elements.description: Tokens only: words, quoted and Unicode identifiers, strings (escape, Unicode and bit strings, and a string continued across a newline, joined as Postgres does), dollar quotes, numbers, parameters, operators, punctuation, comments; anything else is a bad token. Not a parser. Linear time.

elements.name: Reject list
elements.description: The courtesy list as one table: 16 reasons, each with the feature, why it cannot work under transaction pooling and an example, plus the transaction-scoped forms that are allowed. docs/reject-list.md is generated from it. Not a safety mechanism: no guarantee rests on it.

elements.name: Statement classifier
elements.description: Turns one Query message into a work unit. Lexes it, splits it on semicolons and rejects the whole message when any statement uses a reject-list feature (first reason wins); otherwise the unit starts a lease, or continues one inside a transaction. Never refuses a message for being untokenisable: it is marked opaque and forwarded. Sets safe-read from the safe-shape recogniser, shareable (safe-read, outside a transaction, not rejected), hinted (the text begins with /* mg:share */) and the share key (exact text, tenant by config). Counts by class and reason in its own snapshot, with a conservation check.

elements.name: Safe-shape recogniser
elements.description: Decides what may be shared, from the raw bytes alone: it uses neither the lexer nor the classifier and imports nothing. A text fits when it is at most 4,096 bytes of a small alphabet, starts with SELECT, has no word on the stop list, no time word in a string, and calls only functions on the allow-list. Allocates nothing. docs/safe-shape.md is generated from its tables. Stated limit: it cannot see a view, operator or row-level security policy that hides a side effect.

elements.name: Error contract and reply builders
elements.description: One table of 24 rows: each refusal and failure, its reply form, its SQLSTATE, whether anything reached the database, whether a write may have applied, and what happens to the client connection. The reply builder appends the ErrorResponse and the correct end marker for a row and counts replies by row. The discard-until-Sync rule refuses extended-protocol messages. docs/error-contract.md is generated from the table. The engine sends the rows of the walking skeleton, the admission shed row and the pool's rows (breaker open, cancelled while queued, idle in a transaction), and the client session machine the startup rows; the rows of cores not built yet (rate gate and others) are not sent so far.

elements.name: Startup-only test proxy and startup fidelity runner
elements.description: internal/pgwire/pgwiretest. A proxy for tests on simulated streams: the two session machines back to back, one database connection per client, no pool; after login it relays queries and replies through both trackers. A database startup failure reaches the client as FATAL 08006. Also the startup fidelity runner: one script (TLS answers, SCRAM, protocol versions) played against the fake Postgres and compared with Postgres 17's transcript, recorded for CI or live in tier R.

elements.name: Wire scenarios
elements.description: internal/pgwire/pgwiretest/wireworld. 19 named scenarios with their exact checks: the test proxy between simulated clients and the fake Postgres, plaintext and TLS, one-byte delivery, and one startup fault each on the client side (TLS stall, bad hello, smuggled bytes, second TLS request, plaintext refused, wrong password, unknown user) or the database side (silence, connect stall, garbage, reset, connection limit, TLS refused, bad certificate, handshake stall). Each failure must be counted under its one reason within its deadline.

elements.name: Classifier scenarios
elements.description: internal/pgwire/pgwiretest/clsworld. Two named scenarios and a small test gateway on simulated streams: it relays startup to the fake Postgres (trust login, no session machines), classifies each Query, answers a rejected one and every extended-protocol message itself, and forwards the rest. Simulated clients send every reject-list feature, plain and in padded spellings. Checks: each gets 0A000, no rejected statement reaches the fake, and the session's search_path is unchanged.

elements.name: Rate gate (GCRA)
elements.description: Optional outer gate, off by default: a per-tenant rate and burst in integer nanoseconds. Refuses before anything is queued. Rates are divided by the instance count.

elements.name: Tenant table
elements.description: State for tenants that are active now: queue, in-flight count, share, gate state. Created on first use, removed when all-zero, so memory follows active tenants.
plannedNotes: Built in chunk 8 (internal/admission: tenantFor, dropQuiet, evictEmpty and statsFor in queues.go; tenant.go): one entry per tenant with a queue (its ring, rule state, LIFO state and load gauge), created on first use and removed after 16 quiet intervals, its ring reused. At most queue.max_tenants entries: at the cap an empty queue is evicted for a new tenant, and if none is empty the arrival is shed. A tenant's counters outlive its entry, for at most 4,096 tenants; later ones are counted as other. Not built: in-flight count and share (chunk 9), gate state (chunk 10).

elements.name: Per-tenant queues
elements.description: A fixed-capacity ring per tenant, under one total capacity. Age is measured on the oldest item; expired items are swept from the head, at every operation and at the core's own next deadline, and answered at once. A full ring sheds its head, not the arrival; a full total sheds the oldest request of all. Serves newest-first while the rule reports overload (adaptive LIFO), and oldest-first again once the rule has reported no overload for a hold time. Keeps folly's minimum-delay figure as a load gauge, 0 to 100. A queued request the caller refuses (the breaker opened) is counted as a shed with reason breaker and does not mark the queue as shedding.

elements.name: QueueRule
elements.description: The interface both shedding rules implement; chosen by config (queue.rule: timeout or control-law), per instance.

elements.name: Timeout rule
elements.description: Mode 1, from "Fail at Scale": one last-empty timestamp per queue; allowed wait is the short target while a standing queue exists, otherwise the interval. It is evaluated at the instant, on the oldest item, so the first burst after idle gets the interval.

elements.name: Control-law rule
elements.description: Mode 2, from the CoDel paper and RFC 8289: sojourn above target for an interval starts dropping; next drop after interval / sqrt(count), in integer arithmetic (an exact floor). Its checks run at every queue operation and at the core's next deadline, not only at a pop; a drop sheds the oldest request.

elements.name: Comparison arms
elements.description: Plain FIFO and folly's minimum-delay detector, for the head-to-head table. Only tests and the simulator can select them: the config file's parser accepts neither.

elements.name: Dispatcher
elements.description: Chooses whose request runs next: round robin across tenants with waiting work; a tenant's share binds only when the limit is reached; otherwise work-conserving.
plannedNotes: Built in chunk 8 (internal/admission: Dispatcher, OldestFirst and SetDispatcher in queues.go): the interface the queues ask at each pop, and one default that picks the tenant whose head is oldest. Not built: round robin and shares (chunk 9), the limit they bind under (chunk 10).

elements.name: Adaptive limit (AIMD)
elements.description: One integer limit on concurrent leases. Cut by a tenth on a slow statement, a timeout or a connection failure; raised by one when busy. Bounded by a floor, the pool size, a maximum step and a minimum interval. Reads database round-trip time, never queue wait.

elements.name: Admission snapshot
elements.description: Snapshot(): per tenant and total — depth, capacity, oldest-item age, queue-wait histogram, rule state, LIFO switches, sheds by reason, the load gauge, in flight, share, limit and its changes, gate refusals.
plannedNotes: Built in chunk 8 (internal/admission: snapshot.go): per tenant and total — depth, capacity, oldest-item age, queue-wait histogram, rule state, LIFO state and switches, sheds by reason, the load gauge, shedding — with a conservation check (pushes = served + shed + removed + queued). Not built: in flight and share (chunk 9), the limit and its changes, gate refusals (chunk 10).

elements.name: Connection accounting
elements.description: Every database connection is connecting, idle, checking, lent, cleaning or resetting; a closed one is forgotten in the step that issues its close. Invariant: open + connecting never exceeds the cap, which is pool.connections or, when that is omitted, the fleet budget divided by the instance count (rounded down, never zero).

elements.name: Creation limiter
elements.description: Opens connections only on demand: while more requests wait than connections are idle or being prepared. No prefill. Caps concurrent connects and the rate of new connections (consecutive dials at least 1/rate apart; the rate is the fleet's divided by the instance count), so a storm or a cold start cannot flood the database. The breaker's trial dial and the redials after a mass death pass through it too.

elements.name: Lease table
elements.description: Checkout and release. Lends the most recently used idle connection, and never one in doubt. A checkout that cannot lend is refused, so a request never waits inside the pool. Two release policies: always resets after every lease; on-switch tags the connection with its tenant, prefers a connection last held by the same tenant and lends it as is, and resets one that must switch tenants, at checkout. With the re-seed on, every reset carries a new random seed. The engine decides when a lease ends (the status byte) and holds the idle-in-transaction deadline; the pool is told how the lease ended.

elements.name: Check before reuse
elements.description: An idle connection that is suspect, or idle for the check-after-idle time or longer, is sent an empty query before it is lent, off the request path and under its own short deadline; a failed check closes it and costs no client. The suspect rule: any connection-class failure marks every other connection suspect, and only a passed check clears the mark. At most four checks start per checkout.

elements.name: Database-down breaker
elements.description: The one circuit breaker. Counts consecutive connection-class failures only (a failed dial, bytes on an idle connection, the loss of a connection in use); never SQL errors, a polite close of an idle connection, or a failed check that is not its trial. Open: requests are refused at once, no dial is made, and the queued requests are refused. Half-open after a set time: requests are admitted and wait behind exactly one trial — a dial, or a check of an idle connection when the pool is at its cap — sent only when work wants it. A failed trial opens it again.

elements.name: Dirty-connection table
elements.description: What to do with a connection whose lease did not end clean (client gone, idle in a transaction, a statement or write deadline): cancel a statement still running and drain its reply, roll back an open transaction, reset, and wait for the cancel to finish, all inside the clean-up deadline; reuse only after every step succeeded, otherwise close. A lost connection or one with unread bytes is closed. Destroy on doubt.

elements.name: Idle and lifetime reaper
elements.description: Closes a connection that has been idle past its idle timeout, or that is idle and older than its lifetime. Each connection draws its own two limits at dial time, spread by the jitter (10% either way by default), so connections made together do not expire together. Also ends a check, a reset or a clean-up at its deadline. Deadlines fire at equality: what arrives at its deadline is late.

elements.name: Cancel table
elements.description: A client's cancel is accepted only for a lent connection, and the table's own cancels come from the dirty-connection table. Each goes out on a second connection that is outside the cap; at most a set number are in flight. A connection is not lent again until its cancel has finished, and one whose cancel never reported is closed at its next return. The engine, not the pool, maps a client's key data to the connection it holds.

elements.name: Pool snapshot
elements.description: Snapshot(): the caps; open, connecting, idle, lent, checking, cleaning, resetting and suspect, with peaks; dials, failures and waits for the creation rate; closes by reason; checkouts, exhaustion events, lends as is, tenant switches; lease ends and dirty-table outcomes by kind; resets by cause and outcome, re-seeds; checks by result; cancels; breaker state, transitions, trials and failures; lease-time and idle-age histograms. Its check holds the cap and the conservation laws (every dial, checkout, check and cancel ends in exactly one outcome).

elements.name: Join rule
elements.description: Decides whether a shareable request leads a new read or joins one. Strict (default): never join a read already running on the database — join the next one, which starts when the running one ends. Relaxed: join the running read.

elements.name: Flight table
elements.description: In-flight and pending shared reads, keyed by the exact statement text. At most one read per key is on the database at a time. Entries are removed on completion.

elements.name: Waiter set
elements.description: The callers of one flight, counted. Capped. A caller that leaves gets its own error and does not disturb the rest.

elements.name: Flight deadline
elements.description: The flight runs under its own deadline, not any caller's. The database work is cancelled only when the last waiter has left.

elements.name: Shared reply buffer
elements.description: The reply's message bytes, stored once and capped; each recipient gets them with its own end marker. Errors are shared too.

elements.name: Do-not-share list
elements.description: Keys whose reply was too large to share. Bounded and expiring.

elements.name: Coalescer snapshot
elements.description: Snapshot(): flights, hits, waiters per flight, cancellations, overflows by cap, shared errors, table size.

elements.name: Policy
elements.description: The interface the engine asks: given this failure — did anything reach the database, is the breaker open, how much of the deadline is left — may it be retried.

elements.name: Off
elements.description: The default. Never retries.

elements.name: PreForwardOnce
elements.description: Retries at most once, only when nothing reached the database, only within budget, never while the breaker is open, never holding a queue slot or a connection while it waits.

elements.name: Retry budget
elements.description: An integer bucket: each first attempt deposits a tenth of a token, each retry takes one; capped, so credit expires. Retries stay at or below 10% of requests.

elements.name: Retry snapshot
elements.description: Snapshot(): attempts, retries, budget level, deposits, withdrawals, exhaustions, refusals by reason.

elements.name: Event loop
elements.description: internal/sim. One thread, one heap ordered by (time, sequence). An event is a closure, or an opaque handler with an integer code. Step, run until a time, run until quiet. A step budget, typed stall errors (budget spent, time frozen, heap full) and a panic guard, each carrying the REPLAY line.

elements.name: Virtual clock and timers
elements.description: internal/sim. 64-bit nanoseconds that saturate instead of overflowing. Cancellable timers: a cancel removes the event from the heap. A timer marked background does not count in the quiesce check. Time moves only when the loop moves it.

elements.name: Named random streams
elements.description: internal/sim. One generator per (seed, label), so a new draw in one place does not shift any other.

elements.name: Simulated byte streams
elements.description: internal/sim/simnet. Listeners and ordered byte connections with chosen fragmentation (down to one byte), latency per direction, a bounded send window (back pressure), half-close and reset. Its faults: reset, stall, half-open, half-close, chunk, refuse, dial stall, accept-then-silence, and clear. Its own snapshot.

elements.name: Fake Postgres
elements.description: internal/sim/fakepg. Speaks the simple-query subset in real wire bytes with its own framer; login by trust or SCRAM-SHA-256; answers a TLS request S or N and plays the simulated handshake; a max_connections limit with Postgres's refusal; transaction status; a small keyed table with write, statement and transaction logs; service-time models and a capacity limit; cancel requests; every database-side fault (the TLS ones — answers N, a handshake that fails or stalls, a certificate that fails verification — are a setting that can change during a run, not fault kinds); its own snapshots.

elements.name: Clients and tenants
elements.description: internal/sim/workload. Simulated clients grouped in tenants: open-loop arrivals (constant or Poisson) and closed-loop think time, latency measured from the intended send time, uniform, Zipf or fixed keys, transactions of several statements, retries with backoff; login by trust or SCRAM-SHA-256, with a TLS request first when the tenant asks; every client-side fault (the four TLS ones — stall after the request, bad hello, plaintext after the request, a second request — are a per-tenant setting); its own snapshot. A client sends one request at a time; later arrivals wait in its bounded backlog. Also a hand-driven client (Probe) for tests.

elements.name: Test client
elements.description: internal/testclient. A Postgres client with no I/O: bytes in, messages out. Its own framer, a message codec, and a session machine (phase, status byte, key data, parameters) with trust login. It hands the data of each authentication message to its caller, which is how the simulated clients run SCRAM. Used by the simulated clients on simulated streams and by the tier R tests on TCP.

elements.name: Simulated TLS handshake
elements.description: internal/sim/simtls. A handshake as an exchange with an outcome, not cryptography: a 16-byte client hello (or a bad one) and a 16-byte server reply that says completed with a TLS version, bad certificate, or alert. Models the outcome and the duration only.

elements.name: Float generators
elements.description: internal/randdist. The only two functions that use floating point: exponential gaps for Poisson arrivals, and a Zipf generator. Kept outside internal/sim, where float syntax is forbidden.

elements.name: Scenario world
elements.description: internal/sim/world. The scenario type; the driver interface (start, connect, inject, run, observe, stop) and its simulator implementation; five direct baselines with no proxy (500 connections, reconnect burst, 1,000 identical reads, open-loop overload, mixed transactions); the write-log and transaction checks; the fidelity runner, which plays one script against the fake and compares the transcript with Postgres 17's, recorded for CI or live in tier R.

elements.name: Fault schedule and shrinker
elements.description: internal/sim. Timed faults, each recorded in the trace when it is applied. A package registers the fault kinds it can apply. A schedule can be decoded from bytes for the fuzzer, and a delete-one-fault shrinker cuts a failing schedule down. Faults are injected only from outside the code under test.

elements.name: Decision trace and digests
elements.description: internal/sim. Any actor appends a record (time, kind, four integers) in order; the last records are kept in a ring for failure reports. Two digests: one of the trace, one of final state as written by registered state writers. Same seed, same digests.

elements.name: Invariants and quiesce check
elements.description: internal/sim. A package registers its checks. Invariants run after every event (or every Nth); the quiesce checks run at the end of a run: nothing in use, nothing in flight, no timer left. A failed check fails the run.

elements.name: Seeds, replay, sweep
elements.description: internal/sim/simtest. The seed flag and variables, pinned seeds, the sweep over seeds, the run-twice check, the failure report with the trace tail and the REPLAY line. scripts/sweep.sh and scripts/fuzz.sh run the scenario tests and fuzz targets through it; sweep.sh prints one line per scenario and a failure's lines under it (the raw output under VERBOSE=1).

elements.name: cmd/mgsim
elements.description: Lists the named scenarios (toy and world); runs one from a seed outside go test, prints its digests (and the trace on request; for a world scenario also its result table) and exits 1 with the REPLAY line when it fails.

elements.name: Toy echo protocol
elements.description: internal/sim/simtoy. A line-echo client and server with a planted-bug switch, and eleven named scenarios that cover every network fault. Used only to test the harness itself.

elements.name: Snapshot conventions
elements.description: The one common raw export. What every component's Snapshot() returns: a plain struct of monotonic counters and current gauges. No wall-clock time, no map order, no telemetry imports. Nothing else leaves a component; an import rule keeps components and the simulator from importing any adapter.

elements.name: Integer histogram
elements.description: Fixed array, fixed relative error, no allocation on record; record, merge, percentile. Out-of-range values are clamped and counted.

elements.name: Conservation check and gauge
elements.description: A check that a total equals the sum of its parts (for example written = delivered + discarded + in flight); its error names each term and which side is higher. A gauge type that keeps a value and its peak.

elements.name: Snapshot and adapter test helpers
elements.description: internal/obs/obstest. Test plumbing: checks that a snapshot is a plain struct of integers (no time, no map), and that every counter in it moved in at least one test. Also the conformance test every adapter must pass (values, labels, determinism, no kept reference, errors counted), its shared fixture, and the golden-file helper.

elements.name: Metric registry
elements.description: Every exported metric is declared first: component, name, kind (counter, gauge, histogram), which of the four labels it has (tenant, outcome, reason, mode), unit, merge rule (sum, or max for a high-water mark), and whether it is a headline metric. Refuses a bad or repeated name and names that would clash in Prometheus.

elements.name: Instance snapshot
elements.description: What the collector publishes and all an adapter gets: instance id, build, config fingerprint, publish sequence number, and sorted lists of points (integer values) and histogram points. No time, no map.

elements.name: Detail gate
elements.description: The obs.detail setting. Off: the collector folds every tenant into one and drops histogram points, and a detail histogram holds no buckets (a record is one nil check). On: per-tenant rows and full histograms.

elements.name: Collector
elements.description: Components register as sources: their metric declarations, their Snapshot and a mapping from it to points. At each publish it assembles one instance snapshot (with instance id, build and config fingerprint), refusing an undeclared, mistyped, duplicate or missing metric, and hands it to every attached adapter. Keeps the last published snapshot and gives out copies. Counts its own work (publishes, emit errors, export errors per adapter, CSV flushes and drops) as component obs. The only path from a component snapshot to an adapter.

elements.name: Adapter interface
elements.description: The one interface every output form implements: a name, and take the published instance snapshot and produce output. A failed export is counted by the collector and never reaches the publisher. One conformance test for all adapters. Components cannot see past it, so none knows about CSV, DuckDB, OTel or Prometheus.

elements.name: Fleet merge
elements.description: Merges instance snapshots: each metric by its declared rule (sum, or max for a high-water mark), histograms bucket by bucket. Refuses an undeclared metric, a kind or unit clash and an integer overflow. Ratios are never stored, so they are recomputed from the merged counts, never averaged.

elements.name: Health
elements.description: Three states, the worst over a table of named rules, with a reason per rule and a JSON body. The collector rule: degraded before the first publish, and while the latest publish had metric errors or an adapter's export failed. Other rules: degraded while shedding, while the breaker is open, at the limit's floor, or draining; failed only when this instance cannot work (its client listener is down). A database outage is degraded.
plannedNotes: Built in chunks 3, 6, 7 and 8. Chunk 3 (internal/obs: health.go): the three states, the rule table (overall state is the worst rule), the collector rule and the JSON body. Chunk 6: the rule database (internal/obs/enginesrc: degraded while no database connection is usable and the last connect failed) and the rule listener (internal/shell: failed while the client listener is down). Chunk 7: the rule breaker (internal/obs/poolsrc: degraded while the breaker is open or half-open). Chunk 8: the rule admission (internal/obs/admsrc: degraded while a tenant queue shed within the last interval). Not built: the rules for the limit's floor and draining.

elements.name: Prometheus text exporter
elements.description: internal/obs/promtext. Names mg_<component>_<metric>, low-cardinality labels and a bounded tenant label: configured tenants, or the first active ones, up to a cap; quiet tenants lose their slot; the rest are summed as other. Histograms are re-bucketed onto a short bound list. Holds the exposition-grammar checker the tests use.

elements.name: JSON stats exporter
elements.description: internal/obs/jsonstats. The full snapshot, including every active tenant; it decodes back to an equal snapshot.

elements.name: CSV flush adapter
elements.description: internal/obs/csvflush. Flushes snapshots to disk at each publish and at the end of a run, in a stable versioned schema with unbounded per-tenant rows. The testing path: tests assert on the files with no Collector or Prometheus running. Bounded size; drop-and-count at the cap, on a write error and on a full queue. Writes in the caller (simulator and tests) or through a bounded queue that never blocks the caller (real process). Holds the reader and the round-trip check: the final flush read back equals the snapshot.

elements.name: Log-line exporter
elements.description: internal/obs/logline. One structured line per publish: sequence number, instance, build, config fingerprint and the headline metrics. At most 1,024 bytes.

elements.name: OTLP/HTTP push exporter
elements.description: The final adapter and the proxy's end of the production path. Hand-written on the standard library, no SDK. Cumulative sums, gauges, short-list histogram buckets, bounded tenant label. Bounded queue, timeout, drop-and-count when the Collector is down. Lands in the last build chunk and touches no component.

elements.name: Simulator source mappings
elements.description: internal/obs/simsrc. The metric declarations and the snapshot-to-points mappings of the four simulator components that exist: the kernel, simnet, the fake Postgres (its authentication and TLS counters too) and the workload (its startup counters too). It lives here because the simulator packages are frozen; a later component writes the same two functions in its own package.

elements.name: Wire source mapping
elements.description: internal/obs/wiresrc. The metric declarations of component wire and the mapping from the wire snapshot to points. The side is in the metric name (client_..., database_...); labels are reason, outcome and mode; every known label value is emitted, zero included; no tenant label.

elements.name: Classifier source mapping
elements.description: internal/obs/clssrc. The metric declarations of component classifier and the mapping to points from three wire-layer snapshots: the classifier's (statements, by class, rejects by reason, opaque, safe-read, shareable, hinted, share keys), the reply builder's (replies by error-table row, failures) and the discard-until-Sync counters. All counters; every known label value is emitted, zero included; no tenant label.

elements.name: Engine source mapping
elements.description: internal/obs/enginesrc. The metric declarations of component engine and the mapping to points from two snapshots: the engine's, and the shell's (mailbox depth and peak, goroutines, readers and writers, deadlines; names shell_...). Labels are outcome, reason and mode; no tenant label so far. Registers the engine's wire, classifier, pool and admission sources beside its own. Holds the health rule database: degraded while no database connection is usable and the last connect failed or the breaker is not closed; hands on the breaker rule and the admission rule with it.

elements.name: Pool source mapping
elements.description: internal/obs/poolsrc. The metric declarations of component pool and the mapping from the pool snapshot to points: every field of the snapshot, with labels reason (closes, lease ends, dirty-table outcomes), outcome (checkouts, checks) and mode (resets, breaker transitions); no tenant label. The two histograms only with obs.detail on. Holds the health rule breaker: degraded while the breaker is open or half-open.

elements.name: Admission source mapping
elements.description: internal/obs/admsrc. The metric declarations of component admission and the mapping from the admission snapshot to points. Totals always: the rule, capacities, queued, tenant queues, pushes, served, removed, sheds by reason, LIFO switches, queues by rule state, the load gauge, shedding. With obs.detail on: the queue-wait histogram and a row set per tenant, the gateway's first metrics with a tenant label. Holds the health rule admission: degraded while a tenant queue shed within the last interval.

elements.name: Admission head-to-head table
elements.description: scripts/admission-head-to-head.sh and test/analysis/admission-head-to-head. One DuckDB query over the flushed runs of the head-to-head scenarios prints the table: both rules and the two comparison arms at 1.2×, 2× and 10× load, with served-wait percentiles, depth, served, shed, shed by the rule, and idle share. --check reruns the scenarios and requires the output to equal the committed table.

elements.name: Metric catalog and schema document
elements.description: internal/obs/catalog. The registry of every source the product registers, with the load generator's metrics beside them, and the generator of docs/csv-schema.md (columns of the three files and every metric). Its test fails when the committed document differs from the code; scripts/gen-docs.sh regenerates or checks it.

elements.name: Scenario flush harness
elements.description: internal/obs/simrun. Runs a simulator world scenario, a wire scenario, a classifier scenario, or any run handed its simulator and sources (the end-to-end suite's tier S scenarios), with a collector that publishes on the virtual clock and with the CSV, JSON, Prometheus and log adapters attached, then checks every output against the final snapshot. Its tests run the five direct baselines, every wire scenario and both classifier scenarios twice per seed and compare the files byte for byte.

elements.name: SQL assertions and their runner
elements.description: scripts/csv-assert.sh and test/analysis. The runner finds run directories, checks them with guard.sql (schema version, no empty required field, one run id per directory, no empty run), loads views.sql and runs each assertion file; a returned row is a violation. Fails closed and never skips. The assertion files check the direct baselines' counts and, for each wire scenario, that startup failures by reason, TLS requests by answer and handshake failures equal what was injected and sent, and for the classifier scenarios that rejects equal the statements sent and the fake Postgres started only what was forwarded (nothing in the reject-only scenario). For the end-to-end scenarios of both tiers: conservation per instance, the resets against the leases ended and, where the scenario has a fault, error-contract replies by row = faults injected; in tier S also proxy completed = workload completed and replies by row = what the clients saw. For the admission scenarios: conservation (the engine's sheds = the queues' sheds too), served-wait bounds from the histogram buckets, depth, and 53M01 replies = sheds. For the pool scenarios: in every flush open + connecting is at most the cap, every dial and checkout has one outcome, nothing is lent at the end, and each scenario's own claim (the dial rate, the breaker's recovery, the fake's connection peak, no statement left without a reply).

elements.name: Story report
elements.description: scripts/report.sh and test/analysis/report; make report RUNS=<dirs> or SEEDS=N. Reads the flushed files of any set of runs and prints seven sections for people: what the runs prove, how the data was collected, the inputs, coverage (requests by outcome, replies by error-contract row, statements by class, the load generator's totals), every failed assertion in full, every oracle mismatch in full, and a verdict table that ends in one VERDICT line. Runs each scenario's assertion files and five built-in checks of the load generator's numbers. Fails closed; exits 1 on any failed check; the same runs give byte-identical output. The assertions stay the gate.
